signals.title: New In-Memory Database Purpose-Built for AI Agents
signals.excerpt:
SAN MATEO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Neo4j Ⓡ, the world’s leading graph intelligence platform, today released Relate, an AI-native, open source, in-memory and in-process embedded database built in Rust for AI Agents and Agentic Systems. With Relate, AI coding agents can create a database and start building applications in milliseconds.

...

Relate, released as open source under the Apache 2.0 license, brings multihop reasoning capabilities and GraphRAG to AI agents for more accurate results and fewer hallucinations. The database is engineered specifically for the execution loops of autonomous agents. It natively auto-detects agent harnesses and returns structured errors equipped with explicit retryable flags. These flags enable agents to handle exceptions and self-correct without custom parsing logic. Relate enforces a row cap combined with an in-band truncation marker to prevent context window saturation during large retrievals. This constraint ensures agents receive bounded and predictable payloads.

...

The new embedded in-memory database for AI agents deploys seamlessly across Jupyter notebooks, web browsers, software containers, and edge devices. It runs natively wherever agents are at work. The database ships with built-in agent connectivity via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server and a dedicated CLI for direct execution. Relate also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints to provide drop-in support for existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks, and standard developer tooling.

...

Relate delivers sub-millisecond reads in memory to handle the high-frequency read/write cycles of agentic workloads. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity and execute graph traversals simultaneously. The database maintains strict transactional integrity using an in-memory engine with an optional fsync'd write-ahead log for durable stores. It provides native options to flush state to disk for long-term persistence. Relate is 100% openCypher and more than 97% GQL compliant out of the box.

signals.title: MACaQ quantizes 122B model to W4A4 in 64 min on 32.5GB GPU | AI Weekly
signals.excerpt:
## TL;DR

- MACaQ quantizes a 122-billion-parameter model to MXFP4 W4A4 in 64 minutes using only 32.5GB of GPU RAM.
- On Llama-3-8B it matches DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ perplexity in 11 times less quantization time, adding 2.3% overhead on Qwen3-32B in vLLM.
- Treating every linear layer independently removes cross-layer basis-transform propagation and lets calibration stream one layer at a time.

...

MACaQ, a new post-training quantization method, compresses a 122-billion-parameter model to MXFP4 W4A4 in 64 minutes using 32.5GB of GPU RAM, according to a paper on arXiv by Lorenz K. Muller, Philippe Bich, Chiara Boretti, Hyun-Min Chang, Jiawei Zhuang and Lukas Cavigelli. The authors report matching the perplexity of DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ on Llama-3-8B in "11 times less quantization time," while adding only "2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM."

The speed comes from treating every linear layer independently, avoiding the cross-layer propagation of basis transforms that prior W4A4 methods required. "Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time," the paper states.

The method pairs a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform on activations with a new "Flip-Refinement" procedure, described as a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. The authors also apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, which they offer as evidence that the layer-local design generalizes beyond language models.

The abstract publishes no downstream task accuracy numbers and does not identify which 122B model was used for the headline 64-minute result.

signals.title: Compile the Knowledge at Index Time
signals.excerpt:
That repeated work is what RAGFlow 1.0 is built to remove. InfiniFlow now positions the open-source engine as a supply layer for retrieval agents rather than an end-to-end RAG pipeline, and the mechanism behind the repositioning is knowledge compilation: move the understanding from query time to index time. Compile once, when a document arrives, and store the result as artifacts the agent can use directly, instead of re-deriving the same understanding inside every prompt.

...

And there are atomic propositions, the piece the rest of this post is about.

A proposition is a one-sentence fact extracted from the source, paired with a verbatim quote. The quote has to be a contiguous substring of the original text, and that is checked mechanically. A proposition whose quote does not match the source word for word does not count as evidence.

...

What moved the numbers was attaching claim-evidence pairs to the tree's leaves. When the evidence at a leaf is sufficient to answer, the agent answers from the evidence and skips reading the raw chunk entirely. The paper reports that this cuts query tokens by 91% when the evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not — a 38% average reduction, at a measured sufficiency rate near 43% against a break-even of about 2%.

Huawei CSL released MACaQ, an open-source quantization toolkit for local inference and serving. The repository describes MACaQ as model-agnostic software that quantizes and runs text, image, video and audio models with llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and PyTorch.

...

The project states that MACaQ can quantize a 122-billion-parameter model in 64 minutes with 32.5 GB of device memory. Huawei CSL also claims lower perplexity than MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++, or a match to their best Llama 3 8B perplexity with 11 times less quantization time. Lorenz K. Muller, Philippe Bich, Chiara Boretti, Hyun-Min Chang, Jiawei Zhuang and Lukas Cavigelli describe the method in the paper "MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations". These figures come from the repository and the paper; independent benchmarks will show how the method performs across hardware, calibration data and model families.

...

MACaQ spans more than text GGUF workflows. The Diffusers path targets image, video and audio generation with W4A4 quantization and supports models such as black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-klein-4B, Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers and ylacombe/stable-audio-1.0. The llama.cpp path produces 2-bit, 3-bit and 4-bit GGUF files for text models, including Qwen, OLMoE and other dense or mixture-of-experts recipes listed in the repository. The vLLM integration targets text generation and serving with W4A4 or weight-only checkpoints. The PyTorch path targets speech generation with W4A4 checkpoints for models such as Qwen3-TTS and Chatterbox Turbo.

The repository also introduces MACaQ-R, a refinement step for quantized GGUF files. MACaQ-R adjusts weight codes while preserving the native GGUF formats and block scales, so users can run the output with a standard llama.cpp installation. Huawei CSL reports a comparison for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at the same 22.36 GB file size: Unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL reached a KL divergence to FP16 of 0.015731, while MACaQ-R Q4_K_XL reached 0.013367. Lower KL divergence indicates closer agreement with the FP16 reference in that measurement.

...

MACaQ covers several runtimes, yet each path carries constraints. The Ascend section points to CANN pull requests for W4A4 dense and grouped matmul kernels, and the repository states that full-model execution requires integration with an Ascend inference runtime. Saved PyTorch checkpoints load without repeated calibration, while other workflows depend on calibration data and model-specific recipes documented in the project. The code ships under the Apache License 2.0, and bundled third-party components keep their own licenses.

signals.title: Start and Restore GPU Workloads in Seconds with NVIDIA Snapshot | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Start and

...

Nov 10, 2026

...

NVIDIA Snapshot, a new open-source component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, makes initialized GPU workloads reusable across inference replicas—speeding startup and recovery.

When inference demand spikes or a replica fails, available GPUs don’t translate immediately into serving capacity. Initializing an LLM workload—a process known as a cold start—can take minutes, delaying scaling and recovery.

Snapshot is a checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. It captures a fully initialized workload—including CPU and GPU memory—and restores that state on compatible infrastructure, bringing inference capacity online in seconds instead of minutes. Figure 1 shows the startup sequence. Snapshot skips repeated workload initialization; infrastructure provisioning and container image loading remain outside the measured restore path.

...

The following benchmarks show how Snapshot accelerates inference startup across vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM)—with models from 600 million parameters to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models with 1 TB checkpoints on 8 GPUs. Across all tested configurations, Snapshot brings a replica back in under 45 seconds, 8x to 36x faster than a cold start.

...

### Results

The benchmarks show four main findings.

- Restore times stayed under 43 seconds: Across all tested configurations, Snapshot restored replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold start. The largest MoE models, with checkpoints of about 600 GB to 1 TB across eight GPUs, restored in under 43 seconds compared with cold-start times of 6 to 19 minutes.
- Restoring skips more than weight loading: Cold-start time includes loading weights, compiling and autotuning kernels, and capturing CUDA graphs. Snapshot restores the initialized workload, skipping these repeated steps.
- Checkpointing pays off with the first restored replica: In every tested configuration, checkpoint time plus restore time was shorter than a single cold start. Checkpoint creation took 15 seconds to 5.5 minutes, depending on the model and configuration.
- Moving GPU state dominates large restores: For the eight-GPU MoE configurations, restoring GPU state took 18 to 29 seconds. Restoring CPU process state with CRIU took 4.2 to 10.8 seconds.

signals.title: Building Graph-Enhanced GenAI Applications with graphrag-toolkit - KDnuggets
signals.excerpt:
## Introducing graphrag-toolkit

The graphrag-toolkit is an open-source, Apache 2.0-licensed Python toolkit built by AWS Labs specifically to close that gap. It's made up of two components. The first, and the focus of this article, is lexical-graph, a framework for automatically building a hierarchical knowledge graph from unstructured documents and querying it. The second, BYOKG-RAG (Bring Your Own Knowledge Graph), is a separate approach for teams that already have a knowledge graph and want a multi-strategy question-answering layer over it, without re-extracting anything from scratch.

...

This is the technical core worth understanding before writing any code. Per the toolkit's own graph model documentation, a lexical graph organizes extracted content into six connected levels: source, chunk, topic, statement, fact, and entity. Retrieval can hop between any of these levels rather than being stuck retrieving only at the chunk level the way a plain vector store is, which is the structural feature that makes multi-hop questions actually answerable.

...

Here's the actual query mechanism, sourced directly from the toolkit's querying documentation. A user's question first gets embedded, and that embedding runs a top-K similarity search against the vector store to find anchor points: statements or chunks that look relevant on the surface. Those anchors then seed one or more graph traversal queries, which pull in thematically connected content from across the graph, not just the chunks that scored highest on similarity alone. The retrieved content, grouped by topic and source, is then supplied to an LLM alongside the original question to generate the actual answer.

One genuinely current fact is easy to miss: the toolkit also ships an older semantic-guided search strategy, but the documentation states directly that it's likely to be retired in a future release. Traversal-based search is both the current default and the one worth building against today, which is exactly the approach used in the hands-on build below.

...

The lexical-graph can expose a tenant's graph as a callable tool through a Model Context Protocol server, letting an agent browse a catalog of domain-specific graphs and pick the right one for a given question automatically. Multi-tenancy lets you host several separate graphs — different document collections, different users — inside the same underlying graph and vector stores rather than provisioning new infrastructure per tenant. Metadata filtering lets you constrain both indexing and querying to specific document subsets based on tags you attach yourself. And versioned updates handle the real-world case this tutorial's one-shot build ignored entirely: re-ingesting a document that's since changed, archiving the old version automatically rather than leaving stale, contradictory information in the graph.

signals.title: Together AI Unveils FOSCAR to Accelerate LLM Inference on NVIDIA GPUs | Tech Pulse | TheNextGenTechInsider
signals.excerpt:
# Together AI Unveils FOSCAR to Accelerate LLM Inference on NVIDIA GPUs

Researchers have introduced FOSCAR, a kernel library that utilizes affine folding to optimize 2-bit and 4-bit KV cache decoding. The tool provides significant speedups for LLM inference on NVIDIA H100 and B200 architectures.

...

Researchers from Together AI and the University of Sydney have introduced FOSCAR, a kernel library designed to optimize 2-bit and 4-bit key-s-value (KV) cache decoding for large language model (LLM) inference, according to their research paper.

The development addresses a critical bottleneck in low-bit quantization: while compressing the KV cache reduces high-bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic, the instruction-issue throughput required to dequantize each element—specifically applying scale and offset—often limits latency gains. On H100 GPUs, existing fused kernels have been shown to reach less than 31% of peak HBM throughput due to this arithmetic overhead source.

...

FOSCAR utilizes a technique called affine folding to bypass per-element dequantization. Instead of applying scale and offset to every individual value, the kernel applies these transformations to the partial matrix products or the query/value operands.

Key technical specifications include:

- Mathematical Equivalence: Affine folding produces the same attention output as full dequantization while reducing scale-and-offset operations by up to two orders of magnitude source.
- Hardware Optimization: The library features warp-specialized pipelines specifically tuned for NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) architectures, utilizing `wgmma` and `tcgen05` instructions.
- Instruction Efficiency: Optimized bit manipulation allows for direct feeding of KV operands to Tensor Cores, requiring only 1 and 0.19 ALU instructions per element for INT2 on H100 and B200, respectively source.

## Performance Results

Benchmarks demonstrate substantial speedups across modern NVIDIA architectures:

- NVIDIA H100: FOSCAR INT2 and INT4 kernels achieved geometric-mean speedups of $3.36\times$ and $2.83\times$ over the FlashInfer BF16 baseline source.
- NVIDIA B200: The kernels achieved speedups of $2.67\times$ (INT2) and $2.30\times$ (INT4) over FlashInfer BF16 source.
- Serving Throughput: When integrated into the SGLang engine, FOSCAR increased peak aggregate throughput on long-context workloads by up to $170\%$ compared to 2-bit baselines and $341\%$ compared to 16-bit baselines source.

## Availability

The FOSCAR kernel library is open-source and available via GitHub.

signals.title: Introducing OWE-Bench for Long-Horizon Engineering Projects | Mercor Blog
signals.excerpt:
Today we're releasing OpenWorldEngineer (OWE-Bench), a frontier coding benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering and research tasks across software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing.

We built OWE-Bench to test whether AI agents can make real progress on long-horizon engineering projects, ranging from GPU kernels to aircraft design. Every task is graded on unseen cases and scored on a continuous scale. This means that an agent that speeds up a program halfway to the ceiling earns 50% rather than a pass-or-fail zero.

Claude Fable 5.2 tops the current leaderboard with a score of 54.6%, using an average of 211 million tokens per task attempt. GPT-6 Astra follows with a score of 44.2% using 89 million tokens, and Claude Opus 5.5 at 41.6% using 253 million tokens. No model is close to the benchmark ceiling. Fable 5.2 leads all four domains, with Astra within a few points in physical engineering and scientific computing. The benchmark also successfully differentiates between small and large models, with Inkling and Beam only scoring 1.1% and 3.3% respectively.

...

Tasks for OWE-Bench come in two shapes. In scaffolded tasks, the agent starts from a working codebase and pushes a measurable target such as kernel speed, latency, or error. In end-to-end tasks, it builds the whole artifact from a bare environment: a trained model, a data pipeline, a mechanical design. Depending on the task, agents get 4 to 18 hours per attempt (median 8), for 257 agent-hours across one pass over all tasks, on hardware matched to the task, such as a CPU sandbox, NVIDIA H100 or B300. Seven tasks use a GPU.

 

The 26 tasks span four domains:

- Software engineering (8 tasks): databases, data pipelines, interpreters, and layout, such as exactly-once streaming payments ETL into Iceberg tables with alerts under fault injection
- Physical engineering (5 tasks): CAD reconstruction, structural design, and aircraft, such as a parametric Design/Build/Fly electric aircraft scored over 34 hidden flights spanning three missions
- Machine learning (7 tasks): GPU kernels, training, and inference, such as post-training Qwen3-8B on chess tactics through a metered training service, scored on 1,000 private puzzles
- Scientific computing (6 tasks): chemistry and earth-science modeling, such as relocating an earthquake sequence from supplied seismic observations

...

Fable 5.2 leads in every domain. It scores 62.2% in software engineering against 49.7% for Claude Opus 5.5 (+12.2pp), and 54.6% in machine learning against 47.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (+6.8pp). The gap with the next best model is far smaller in physical engineering (59.6% vs. 57.3%) and scientific computing (40.2% vs. 39.4%), where GPT-6 Astra is within the margin of error.

signals.title: Scaling AI agents with open standards: Kurtis Van Gent on MCP and Agent Skills joining the AAIF | Google Open Source Blog
signals.excerpt:
Building production AI agents requires more than a capable reasoning model. Agents need a reliable way to connect to external systems and data, and they need procedural domain knowledge so they know how to use those tools safely without exhausting their context window.

Over the past year, open source communities have rallied around two complementary open standards to solve these challenges: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for connecting agents to live tools, and Agent Skills for loading procedural instructions and scripts on demand. Following Anthropic's donation of the Agent Skills specification to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) alongside MCP, engineers from Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and the wider ecosystem are now co-maintaining the standard under vendor-neutral governance.

...

At the time, most database conversations focused on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using vector search. However, our team believed that agents and tools held the most interesting potential for large language models (LLMs) going forward. We immediately hit two scaling challenges: Google Cloud supports more than 15 different databases across its portfolio, and new open source agent frameworks (starting with LangChain and LlamaIndex) were emerging every week.

That created a classic N-by-M integration problem between many clients and many data hosts. To solve it, we started GenAI Toolbox for Databases (now MCP Toolbox for Databases) as an open source framework for building and serving tools. We built our own server, clients, and protocol to standardize how agents look up and invoke database tools. Back then, agent terminology wasn't common vernacular yet, so every talk I gave had to start with three to five slides explaining what agents and tools actually were.

...

Agent Skills introduced a remarkably simple, effective pattern for solving that problem through progressive disclosure. By loading only a lightweight YAML frontmatter name and description at startup, and pulling the full `SKILL.md` instructions, reference files, or scripts into context only when a task requires them, Agent Skills commoditized context the same way MCP commoditized tools.

While some observers initially viewed MCP and Agent Skills as competing approaches, they have always been complementary: Agent Skills package domain expertise into modular chunks that teach an agent how to approach a problem, while MCP provides the live execution interface to carry it out. Today, the broader ecosystem has converged on combining them, including efforts around Agent Plugins and proposals for serving Agent Skills over MCP so platform maintainers can distribute domain instructions and live tools together.

...

At the platform level, our Google Cloud Databases team pairs MCP and Agent Skills together inside our Agent Plugins. When a developer using Antigravity connects to a PostgreSQL database on Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, they can install the corresponding Cloud SQL or AlloyDB plugin. From MCP, the agent gets a list of safe actions it can take against the database. From the bundled Agent Skills, it gets step-by-step instructions on how to use those tools for specific tasks, like provisioning an instance or configuring Identity and Access Management (IAM) database authentication securely—and because both specifications are open standards, the same `SKILL.md` and MCP pattern works across any open source database or agent harness.

...

Kurtis Van Gent: If you want to start authoring portable skills today, the documentation at agentskills.io walks through creating your first `SKILL.md` package in just a few minutes, and you can explore Google's open source catalog of developer skills at github.com/google/skills (along with our engineering retrospective on how we ship Google Agent Skills like products).

signals.title: 9 open-source tools that give AI coding agents real context
signals.excerpt:
TL;DR: "context" means three different things for an agent: the structure of your code, the docs of other people's libraries, and plain fast search. Pick one tool per job instead of one tool for everything.

...

### 1. Graphify: a knowledge graph of your repo 

Graphify (Apache-2.0, ~145k ⭐) turns a codebase, plus its docs, SQL schemas, configs and PDFs, into a queryable knowledge graph. Parsing is local and deterministic (AST, no embeddings, no vector store), and every edge is tagged `EXTRACTED` (read straight from the source) or `INFERRED` (resolved by Graphify), so you can see why two things are connected.

...

pip install graphifyy
gr

...

```

You get a `graph.json`, an interactive `graph.html`, and a `GRAPH_REPORT.md` with the most-connected "god nodes" and Leiden communities (your subsystems). It runs as a `/graphify` skill in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Gemini CLI, and there's an MCP server via `graphifyy[mcp]`. If you'd rather not run anything locally, the hosted version is at app.graphify.com.

...

Probe: AST-aware search with zero indexing 

Probe (Apache-2.0, ~740 ⭐) is the smallest project on this list and punches well above its size. It combines ripgrep speed with Tree-sitter parsing, takes Elasticsearch-style boolean queries ranked with BM25, and returns whole functions instead of random line fragments. No embedding model, no index step.

...

### 7. Claude Context: semantic search over your code 

Claude Context (MIT, ~13k ⭐) from Zilliz is an MCP server that indexes your codebase into a vector database (Milvus or Zilliz Cloud) so the agent can search by meaning. It's the most "classic RAG" pick here, and it needs a vector DB and an embedding provider to run.

Use it when your questions are fuzzy ("where do we handle retries?") and you're fine running a vector store.

...

### 9. GitMCP: any GitHub repo as an MCP server 

GitMCP (Apache-2.0, ~8.5k ⭐) is a free, remote MCP server. Point your agent at `https://gitmcp.io/{owner}/{repo}` and it can read that project's docs and code, even if the model has never seen it. There's also a generic `gitmcp.io/docs` endpoint for switching between repos.

Use it when you're working against a niche library with no docs in the model's training data.

## How I'd combine them 

- One structure tool for your own repo: Graphify for relationships across code and docs, or Serena for symbol-level navigation.
- One search tool: ast-grep for exact syntax, Probe for ranked results, Claude Context if you want semantic search.
- One docs tool: Context7 for popular libraries, GitMCP for everything else.

signals.title: AMD Quark quantizes Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to UINT4 for 128 GB Ryzen AI Halo edge deployment
signals.excerpt:
AMD's Quark quantization toolkit enables Qwen3.8-Flash-Next to run on Ryzen AI Halo's unified memory by compressing expert weights to UINT4 and replacing the 51 GB FP8 n-gram table with a 1.3 GB calibrated per-token lookup, cutting checkpoint storage from ~130 GB to ~80 GB.

...

AMD has published a technical evaluation demonstrating how its Quark quantization framework can fit the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next large language model onto consumer-grade Ryzen AI Halo hardware with 128 GB of unified memory. The approach combines activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) to compress routed expert weights to 4-bit unsigned integers (UINT4) with a novel replacement for the model's massive n-gram lookup table. Rather than loading the ~51 GB FP8 n-gram table, AMD tested a calibrated per-token table of only ~1.3 GB that supplies token-specific vectors without local context dependency, plus a zero-lookup baseline for comparison.

The evaluation measures accuracy tradeoffs across thinking and non-thinking modes on benchmarks including MMLU-Pro, coding tasks, and parallel tool-calling. Results show that several thinking-mode scores remain stable even without the full n-gram table, while the calibrated per-token table recovers most of the accuracy loss from zero lookup on non-thinking benchmarks. This work addresses a concrete deployment constraint: unified memory architectures like Ryzen AI Halo cannot offload the n-gram table to separate CPU memory without consuming the same shared pool, making table compression essential for leaving room for the KV cache and runtime buffers.

...

- UINT4 AWQ expert quantization: AMD Quark applies activation-aware weight quantization with group size 128 to the model's routed expert weights, reducing precision from BF16 to 4-bit unsigned integers as the foundation for edge deployment.
- N-gram table architecture: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next uses bigram and trigram hashing at Layer 2 to retrieve learned vectors from a context-dependent table, distinct from ordinary token embeddings; this table contributes ~102 GB in BF16 or ~51 GB in FP8 to checkpoint storage.
- Calibrated per-token replacement (U): A ~1.3 GB table providing one fixed vector per token ID, independent of preceding context, replaces the full n-gram lookup; ordinary token embeddings, output head, and downstream layers remain unmodified.
- Memory-constrained deployment target: Ryzen AI Halo's unified memory architecture means CPU/GPU memory is not separable; the ~130 GB FP8-table checkpoint leaves insufficient headroom for OS, KV cache, and runtime buffers on 128 GB systems.
- Accuracy evaluation scope: Tests cover xhigh reasoning-effort thinking mode, MMLU-Pro, coding benchmarks, and parallel tool-calling with response-length analysis; the calibrated U table recovers most non-thinking accuracy loss versus zero lookup while maintaining several thinking-mode scores.

signals.title: RadixArk team describes serving Meta’s Muse Spark Open on one TPU host | AI.info
signals.excerpt:
The RadixArk team describes running Meta’s 816-billion-parameter Muse Spark Open on a single TPU v7 host using SGLang-TorchTPU. Its post details a megakernel, attention and expert-processing changes, and results on the AgentX benchmark.

...

A post by Haolin Fu, Xiaoyu Zhang, Junyan Xu, Wangyuan Zhang, Haoguang Cai and the RadixArk Team describes serving Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on one TPU v7 host with four chips. The authors write, “We serve Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, on a single TPU v7 host of four chips, with SGLang running on the TorchTPU PyTorch backend.” Their post describes SGLang-TorchTPU with Pallas kernels handling performance-critical work.

The post says Muse Spark Open has about 42 billion active parameters per token. Its 62 decoder layers are all mixture-of-experts layers, and each layer routes a token to eight of 256 experts.

...

The central change is a megakernel: one Pallas program on each device handles all 62 layers of a decode or verification step. SGLang continues to run the embedding, draft model, KV-cache write, language-model head and sampling around that program, the post says.

For a single request, the megakernel takes 1.95 milliseconds per output token, compared with 3.78 milliseconds on the native path, a 1.94-times speedup. Figure 4 measures the verify-step comparison with DFlash2 speculative decoding on GSM8K using an earlier Muse Spark checkpoint. The RadixArk team reports a 1.85-times speedup for two concurrent requests; the gain narrows as concurrency increases.

...

For the 1-million-context version of SemiAnalysis’s AgentX coding benchmark, the post reports a range from 433 output tokens per second per request at 6,101 tokens per second per chip, to 25,906 tokens per second per chip at 95 tokens per second per request. Every TPU result shown finished requests within 47 seconds at the 90th percentile.

The authors describe AgentX as based on 393 opt-in Claude Code sessions, replaying request lengths, shared prefixes, tool pauses and subagent structure with synthetic tokens replacing the original content. The comparison uses the benchmark’s 1-million-context trace set, where prompts reach about 990,000 tokens; throughput counts both input and output tokens.

signals.title: Pipeline Parallelism is here: 8x faster than Apple’s WWDC26 fine-tuning
signals.excerpt:
Announcement · November 11, 2026

# Pipeline Parallelism is here: 8x faster than Apple’s WWDC26 fine-tuning

One 48 GB MacBook Pro ran Apple’s WWDC26 fine-tuning faster than Apple’s four M3 Ultra Mac Studios. Four MacBook Pros ran it more than 8× faster.

We are a small team, twelve months, our own mathematics, and a Tensor Engine built from the ground up. This is what it does.

1,440.8 tokens/s · NukeTorch, one MacBook Pro M5 Max

tokens/s · Apple’s WWDC26 run, four M3 Ultra (Apple’s figure)

5,358.5 tokens/s · NukeTorch, four MacBook Pro M5 Max

8×+ faster than Apple’s WWDC26 run, every run

Today we also release NukeTorch for one Mac as a free download, so you can test our speed yourself.

...

At WWDC 2026, Apple fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B with MLX: about 180 tokens/s on one M3 Ultra Mac Studio, and about 600 on four. We ran Apple’s recipe, with Apple’s own commands, on MacBook Pros.

| | Apple, WWDC26 | NukeTorch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One machine | ~180 tokens/s One M3 Ultra Mac Studio | 1,440.8 tokens/s One MacBook Pro M5 Max, 48 GB |
| Four machines | ~600 tokens/s Four M3 Ultra Mac Studios | 5,358.5 tokens/s Four MacBook Pro M5 Max, 48 GB each |
| Method on four machines | Data parallel | Pipeline parallel |
| 1,000 steps on four machines | About 40½ minutes at that speed | Under 5 minutes |

The machines differ, and Apple’s figures are the ones spoken in its session. We did not run Apple’s setup. One machine trains 4 examples per step and four machines train 16, as in Apple’s two commands. Every four-Mac run of ours was more than 8× Apple’s figure. The slowest was 8.45×.

signals.title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, finding that structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption.

Abhishek Bansal, Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotStar, compared filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The team evaluated the approaches using subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, alongside a custom question-answering harness for JioHotstar's codebase. The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability.

...

The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked out repositories and standard search and file operations, remained competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which provides indexed text search, symbol definitions, references, and file reads, performed better than the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while also costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results.

CodeScaleBench showed a different pattern. Semantic retrieval helped more when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions and map them to implementation details that were not obvious from exact text or symbol searches. The findings suggest that retrieval approaches should be selected according to task characteristics rather than treated as interchangeable solutions.

...

JioHotstar's evaluation did not identify a single retrieval approach that performed best across all tasks. Instead, JioHotstar recommends retaining filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems and semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. JioHotStar engineering team also emphasizes measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to determine whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. The findings highlight the importance of matching retrieval capabilities to the programming task and how the agent navigates the codebase.

signals.title: Huawei's MACaQ-R beats Unsloth's Qwen3.6-35B-A3B GGUF by re-coding Unsloth's own file: we diffed the two — sysnote
signals.excerpt:
Huawei's Computing Systems Lab in Switzerland has open-sourced MACaQ, the quantizer behind its paper "MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations" (arXiv:2611.10649, by Lorenz K. Muller, Philippe Bich, Chiara Boretti, Hyun-Min Chang, Jiawei Zhuang and Lukas Cavigelli). The repository, huawei-csl/MACaQ, has backends for llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and plain PyTorch, and the headline for local-model users is a single file published on November 11: `huawei-csl/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MACaQ-R-GGUF`, a Q4_K_XL GGUF that runs in stock llama.cpp and, per Huawei, gets closer to the full-precision model than Unsloth's popular quant of the same size.

The comparison in the README is precise enough to check:

| Model | GGUF size | KL divergence to FP16 ↓ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsloth UD-Q4_K_XL | 22.36 GB | 0.015731 |
| MACaQ-R Q4_K_XL | 22.36 GB | 0.013367 |

That is 15% lower KL divergence at an identical size. What the table doesn't spell out is that the two files are not competitors in the usual sense. MACaQ-R is not a new quantization of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B; it is Unsloth's file with some of its numbers changed.

...

Because nothing about the format changes, the result needs no new kernels and no fork: `llama cli -m` on a stock install loads it. In principle the same post-pass could be run over other people's K-quant MoE GGUFs, and the repo invites exactly that. Two caveats follow from the same fact. First, the improvement is relative to the file it started from, so it says nothing about how MACaQ-R would compare with a quant built differently from scratch. Second, the 15% is Huawei's own KL measurement on its own evaluation text; the README asks users to keep evaluation inputs separate from calibration, but no independent number exists yet, and KL divergence is a proxy rather than a task score. The Hugging Face repo showed zero downloads when we checked.

...

The paper itself is mostly about something else: an MXFP4 W4A4 method that quantizes weights and activations, treats every linear layer independently, and keeps a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online for each layer's activations instead of propagating transforms across layers. That layer-local design is what lets it stream through a model one layer at a time; the authors report quantizing a 122B-parameter model in 64 minutes with 32.5 GB of GPU memory, 2.3% end-to-end overhead over plain MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM, and lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ on Llama-3-8B, matching their best result with 11× less quantization time. The same code quantizes FLUX.2-klein-4B, Wan2.2 video models and Qwen3-TTS, which is the "model agnostic" in the name. Those W4A4 checkpoints need MACaQ's own runtime or kernels, unlike the MACaQ-R GGUF.

signals.title: China Telecom Launches Xing4.0-29B-A4B Mixture-of-Experts Model | Tech Pulse | TheNextGenTechInsider
signals.excerpt:
China Telecom has released the Xing4.0-29B-A4B MoE model, trained entirely on Ascend NPUs using the MindSpore framework. The model features 29 billion parameters and is optimized for agentic workflows and long-context stability.

...

China Telecom Artificial Intelligence Technology Co., Ltd. has released Xing4.0-29B-A4B, a next-generation large language model (LLM) within the Xing series, according to the project's GitHub repository. This Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model features 29 billion total parameters, with only 4 billion activated per token, optimizing the balance between computational efficiency and model intelligence.

The release marks a significant milestone in domestic AI development, as it is the first model of this scale trained entirely on the Ascend NPU platform using the MindSpore framework. By leveraging deep co-optimization with Ascend 910C clusters, the developers achieved a training throughput improvement of approximately 96% compared to out-of-the-box performance as detailed in the official documentation.

...

The architecture is specifically engineered for agentic workflows and long-context stability. Key technical specifications include:

- Architecture: Built on an mHC + MLA + MTP framework to support multi-step planning and tool calling source.
- Context Window: Natively supports a 256K context length, with extensibility up to 512K.
- MoE Configuration: Utilizes 64 routed experts with 4 active experts per token and 1 shared expert.
- Hardware Optimization: Employs Ascend C mHC fused operators and DVM automatic graph-operator fusion for enhanced NPU efficiency.

## Performance Results

In comparative benchmarking, Xing4.0-29B-A4B demonstrates superior performance in specialized coding and agentic reasoning tasks. According to benchmark data provided by the developers:

- SWE-bench Verified: Achieved a score of 75.0, significantly outperforming Gemma4-26B-A4B (53.0).
- Terminal-Bench 2.1: Scored 57.5, surpassing Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (51.5).
- Claw-Eval: Reached 76.55, leading the comparison group.
- DeepresearchBII: Recorded 60.80, higher than both Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (59.70) and Gemma4-26B-A4B (39.30).

...

The model is highly compatible with the existing open-source ecosystem. It supports fine-tuning via LLaMA-Factory and MindFormers, and inference through SGLang, vLLM, and llama.cpp (via GGUF). Native support for Xing4.0 has been merged into the llama.cpp mainline and SGLang mainline as of November 2026 according to the repository updates.

signals.title: From enterprise context to action: Genie Agents now analyze more data sources to transform your work | Databricks Blog
signals.excerpt:
# From enterprise context to action: Genie Agents now analyze more data sources to transform your work

Genie Agents now reason across your Lakehouse data, unstructured documents and enterprise tools in a single conversation.

...

Summary

- Analyze unstructured data: Ask questions across governed tables and thousands of documents in Unity Catalog volumes, with page-level citations. Now in Public Preview.
- Connect and take action: Pull in app data with Lakeflow and use native MCP connectors (now GA) to read from tools like Jira, Slack and Google Drive and act on them.
- Share beyond your company: Use OpenSharing (beta) and Genie Clean Rooms (beta) to give partners and customers a governed agent without exposing the data behind it.

...

Genie Agents started as the fastest way to turn business questions into SQL insights. Today, they have evolved into something bigger: a no-code agent that understands your entire business context. With unstructured data analysis and new MCP connectors, Genie Agents can conduct high-quality business analytics, analyze large volumes of documents and connect to your enterprise tools to take action on your behalf.

...

Building these workflows at scale also requires developing custom RAG, including advanced parsing capabilities, building a separate AI Search endpoint, writing an embedding pipeline, summarizing document insights and passing those summaries to a supervisor agent framework with robust permissions.

...

Genie Agents simplify unstructured data work for your team by automatically handling document parsing, indexing and context retrieval to return high-quality results along with specific citations.

Genie Agents use our custom AI document parsing function to read each file the way a person would. They recognize tables, figures, headers and footers and preserve the surrounding context. Because parsing and indexing run at scale, one agent can work through thousands of files, searching for the ones relevant to your question and citing the exact page for each answer.

...

Agent builders can attach Unity Catalog Volumes containing PDFs, documents, slide decks or images directly to a Genie Agent. The agent retrieves the file content most relevant to the question and adds it to its context. The agent then reasons over that content together with any structured data to generate an answer with citations. These citations can point to the specific page of the source file. Users can ask questions across a specific volume, multiple volumes and structured data in the same conversation.

Unstructured data analysis runs in Agent mode, using multi-step reasoning to retrieve and analyze the most relevant file content. It respects Unity Catalog permissions, meaning users only see files they have access to, and supports content search indexing for faster, higher-quality retrieval across large volumes of data.

...

Take action with MCP connectors. Native MCP connectors, now GA, let agents get context from tools like Slack, Google Drive, Google Calendar, Gmail, Glean, Atlassian, Github and Microsoft 365. Genie Agents can also act by creating tickets, updating records and posting messages. Authors can choose exactly which tools each agent can use, and every connector is governed through Unity Gateway.

...

Genie Agents are built for this work. They can be scoped for a business domain or workflow with its own data, files, tools and instructions. Teams can define this agent once, then deploy it through APIs, custom applications and automated workflows. Genie One and Genie MCP can also call these agents when a task needs deeper investigation.

signals.title: LMSYS Org Launches SGLang Consortium with NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google, Meta, Cloudflare, Modal and RadixArk to Advance Open-Source AI Inference - LMSYS Org
signals.excerpt:
SAN FRANCISCO, November 12, 2026 — LMSYS Org, the nonprofit behind the open-source AI engine SGLang, today launched the SGLang Consortium with founding members NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google, Meta, Cloudflare, Modal and RadixArk, who will work with SGLang’s maintainers to help shape the project’s roadmap and advance open-source AI inference. The consortium was announced in the opening keynote of the inaugural SGLang Summit in San Francisco.

...

Inference is expected to account for roughly two-thirds of all AI compute in 2026, up from about half in 2025, according to Deloitte. The inference engine determines how fast and cost-effectively that compute runs on each company’s hardware. SGLang, the full-stack inference engine for frontier AI and part of the PyTorch ecosystem, runs on hundreds of thousands of GPUs and powers some of the largest production inference deployments in the world, for companies including Meta, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Thinking Machines Lab, Cloudflare, Reflection and Modal.

The consortium gives its members a standing forum to discuss emerging inference trends with SGLang’s maintainers and turn shared priorities into joint engineering work, focused on frontier model support, reasoning and multimodal workloads, distributed inference and hardware optimization. Each founding member will designate a technical representative and join two roadmap meetings a year, contributing through engineering expertise, deployment feedback, testing resources or joint development. Working groups may collaborate between meetings, with public updates on roadmap direction and progress. SGLang’s maintainers keep responsibility for technical decisions and code acceptance, and the project stays open to the entire community.
